t: The movement held that black liberation would come not only from political and structural change but from a psychological transformation in which black people believed in the value of their blackness.
It asked white allies to understand and support, but not to lead, and it defined black to include South Africans of Indian descent and other people of colour.

Many of its leaders were banned or imprisoned and its organisations were outlawed in 1977, a month after Steve Biko died in police custody, yet its language and strategy spread through most corners of black South African politics.
dyk: By 19 June 1976, three days after the Soweto uprising began, 123 key members of the movement had been banned and assigned to internal exile in remote rural districts.
ev: An Anglican meeting convened under Archbishop Robert Selby Taylor leads to the University Christian Movement, which becomes the vehicle for Black Consciousness
Steve Biko, Barney Pityana, Mapetla Mohapi, Mamphela Ramphele and Bennie Khoapa establish the Black Community Programmes as self-help groups
The government begins to clamp down, and virtually the entire leadership of SASO and the Black Community Programmes is banned
Leaders are arrested under the Terrorism Act after rallies in support of the FRELIMO government in Mozambique
Black children march in Soweto against Afrikaans-medium teaching and security forces kill 176 protesters by the official count
Steve Biko dies in police custody on 12 September
On 19 October, known as Black Wednesday, 19 groups associated with the movement are declared illegal
The Azanian People's Organisation is formed and its chairman and secretary are soon detained under the Terrorism Act

f.where: South Africa, especially its universities, townships and churches, with strong activity in Durban and Soweto; community programmes in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal
f.period: emerged in the mid-1960s; University Christian Movement 1966; Black Community Programmes 1970; strikes and protests 1972–1973; bans and arrests from 1973; Soweto uprising 1976; Biko's death and the banning of its organisations 1977; AZAPO founded 1978; ideas and successor groups continuing today
f.figures: Steve Biko, its founder and primary leader; Barney Pityana; Mamphela Ramphele; Bennie Khoapa; Mapetla Mohapi, director of the Zimele Trust Fund; Aubrey Mokoape and Patrick Lekota, among the SASO nine; the poets Mongane Serote and Mafika Gwala
f.outcome: it did not bring down apartheid and its organisations were banned in 1977, but its ideas spread through most of black South African politics and the Azanian People's Organisation (AZAPO) persists
